title: KenKen: Sudoku's arithmetic cousin
description: KenKen keeps Sudoku's tidy grid but adds little cages with sums and differences to solve. It was invented by a teacher who wanted maths practice to feel like play.

body.heading: A grid with cages
paragraphs: A KenKen grid — start with four-by-four — must be filled so that every row and column contains the numbers 1 to 4 exactly once, just like Sudoku. The twist is the cages: groups of cells outlined in bold, each labelled with a target number and an operation, like “7+” or “2÷”.

The numbers inside a cage must combine, using that operation, to make the target. Unlike rows and columns, a cage may repeat a number if the cells sit in different rows and columns. The name KenKen is often explained as “cleverness squared” in Japanese.

body.heading: A teacher's invention
paragraphs: KenKen was created in 2004 by Tetsuya Miyamoto, a Japanese schoolteacher whose classroom philosophy was “the art of teaching without teaching”. His pupils learned arithmetic by wrestling with puzzles rather than drills, and the cages were his way of hiding practice inside a game.

Start solving with the single-cell cages — those are gifts. Then look for cages with only one possible combination: in a four-by-four, a two-cell cage marked “4×” must be 1 and 4, because no other pair multiplies to 4 within range.

body.heading: Try it: a four-by-four mindset
paragraphs: Before writing any number, list for each cage what combinations could possibly fit. Cross combinations off as rows and columns fill up. KenKen rewards this patient bookkeeping more than guesswork.

Ready to invent? Draw a blank four-by-four, fill it with a valid arrangement of numbers, then draw cages over it and calculate each cage's target. Swap with a friend: setter and solver both learn something different.

takeaway: KenKen hides arithmetic practice inside a logic puzzle — every cage is a tiny sum wearing a disguise.
